pillar_reactions.evidence: Presented from 00:29:07 — a Zoom design session with Trevor, three to four sessions a week at 30 to 40 minutes, strength, conditioning and mobility in every workout, 5 to 10 minute mobility protocols for the working day, and the six-month self-sufficiency frame. Asked for questions the prospect said "No, that sounds great" and immediately mapped it onto what he already knows: "I don't know if you've heard of Mike Matthews, Muscle for Life. I've, you know, I read his books and whatnot, and I kind of learned a lot about this, and I've sort of been doing my own programs since then. So I'm very familiar with that idea." Accepted rather than enthusiastic — he agreed with the concept but engaged with it as something he already understood, and asked nothing about how it would work for him. The one place he might have pushed, his limited shoulder range of motion, he raised earlier and never revisited.

Presented at 00:33:58 as no calorie counting and no tracking, built on what, when and how much, with an eight-hour eating window and a weekly free meal. The rep himself framed it as already solved — "From what I'm hearing from you, you're already doing very good" — and the prospect confirmed with no questions: "No, I've done intermittent fasting, I've done like a 23-hour fasting, one-hour eating window, I've done, you know, I've done multi-day fasts, so I'm very comfortable with different styles of eating. I don't, I can control hunger, you know, it doesn't bother me." This is the pillar that added the least. The prospect is more experienced with the mechanism than the presentation assumed, and the rep did not adapt or find a harder edge — for instance he had already identified his own gap ("long-term, I need to become more, do more meal prep. And have some increased variety") and the pillar never addressed it.

Presented at 00:36:44 as the app, weekly in-app check-ins covering training, sleep and recovery, video form review, and Trevor's private cell number with an instruction to over-communicate — including explicit handling of travel: "when you're going to be, for example, traveling to Korea or somewhere, let him know. He will adjust the program accordingly, so you don't fall off." The prospect tied it directly to his own circumstances rather than just agreeing: "Well, it sounds fantastic. It sounds, you know, like custom, you know, I would be able to get a lot of support. And especially later on, my work schedule becomes more variable, it'll probably be very helpful." This was the strongest reaction of the three and it is the pillar that justifies the fee for a prospect who can already programme himself — worth noting that the rep landed it by mirroring the schedule constraint the prospect had opened the call with.

anchors.raw: That's very reasonable for that amount of help.
anchors.note: Volunteered in the same breath as hearing $6,000, before any justification was offered. The strongest possible price signal and a clean marker of the_optimizer posture — the number was read as proportionate rather than as a barrier. The hesitation that followed was about cash flow timing, not about worth, which is why the split resolved it in about two minutes.

anchors.raw: I'm taking a 40% pay cut to start flight control. So, At a time when I make $146,000 a year right now, flight control starts at $100,000. So I've got to be wise with my finances right now.
anchors.note: The number actually sitting in his head when he heard $6,000 was not a competitor's price, it was a $46,000 income reduction landing within months. This is the whole objection, and it only surfaced because the rep isolated with "You're 100% sure on this?" Had P6b been run before the price, it would have surfaced earlier and been easier to work with.

anchors.raw: I don't know if you've heard of Mike Matthews, Muscle for Life. I've, you know, I read his books and whatnot, and I kind of learned a lot about this, and I've sort of been doing my own programs since then.
anchors.note: A functioning free substitute already in place — book-based self-programming that he credits with getting him from significantly overweight to one of the fittest people in his office. This is the same structural pattern the playbook already logs as a known gap from the Badrane Hriouch call, except here it never became an objection because the prospect never raised it as one. The rep also never neutralised it, so the $6,000 is resting on accountability alone, unstated.

anchors.raw: I work out at home. I have a home gym that's pretty well. I'm stocked with what I need.
anchors.note: Mild. He has already spent on equipment and already trains at home, so the programme's convenience argument is partly pre-satisfied. The rep turned it into a positive by leaning on minimal-equipment simplicity, and the prospect agreed ("I don't want a lot of equipment"), but the unresolved practical consequence showed up at 00:42:26 when he asked what to actually buy and was deferred to Trevor.

anchors.raw: I paid out of pocket. went to school and got certification to do this 13 years ago, right? So I've got an FAA license to do this job that I went and got 13 years ago.
anchors.note: A demonstrated history of paying upfront out of pocket for a credential with a long deferred payoff. Directly supportive of a six-month investment framing, and unused by the rep.
